# Can AI Help a Small Instagram Creator Reach the World?


By OpenTools Team


·


November 10, 2026


Devin Halbal was traveling through Japan when she posted a video repeating "sushi kudasai." It was a joke, not a strategy. Then people started recognizing her on the street in Japan and South Korea, repeating the phrase back and turning up at meetups.


Samuel Dohmen arrived at the same place from the other direction. The German creator's dancing videos, set to "Vielleicht Vielleicht," found an audience abroad. Thousands of women began commenting, making fan edits, and calling him "Filay." A meme formed around a person who had never planned to be one.


Neither story came out of a marketing plan. Both videos reached people nobody had targeted.


That is the part worth watching now, because Instagram has been adding translation and analytics tools that make this kind of accident easier to understand, and to some extent easier to repeat.


## **How Instagram Helps Small Accounts Reach New Audiences**


Instagram does not reserve Reels for existing followers. As[TechCrunch reported](https://techcrunch.com/2024/04/30/instagram-is-updating-its-ranking-systems-to-surface-more-content-from-smaller-original-creators/) , eligible original Reels can start with a small audience that includes non‑followers. If those viewers respond, the video may be shown to larger groups.


It works like circles spreading outward. A Reel finds a few people interested in its subject, and their reaction helps decide whether it travels further.


Geography rarely stops the process. A cooking tutorial filmed in Italy can hold someone in Brazil. A home makeover shot in Germany can find viewers in Japan. Visual formats travel well partly because people do not need to speak the creator's language to follow what is happening.


That early response is why some creators look for a stronger start. Some use regional services such as IGComment, where they can[buy Instagram likes](https://igcomment.com/buy-instagram-likes/) for the US, Germany, France, and other markets. Those packages raise the visible number. They do not guarantee that Instagram will recommend the post in those countries, because distribution still depends on how the platform matches content to viewers and how those viewers react.


Which is roughly how a German dancing video ends up with a fan base abroad.


## **Meta AI Is Breaking the Language Barrier**


The more practical change is Reels translation. **Meta AI** can translate spoken audio, produce a dub that keeps characteristics of the creator's voice, and synchronize lip movements to the new language.


Support has grown to include French, German, Italian, Japanese, and Korean, alongside English, Spanish, Portuguese, and Hindi.


For a small creator, that removes work that used to be unavoidable. Someone who films furniture restoration in English can let a French‑speaking audience follow the same video without recording anything twice. In supported settings, Instagram can also present translated audio automatically based on a viewer's language.


The feature is available to eligible public accounts in supported regions, and creators can control the settings and preview translations where that option exists.


There are limits. Slang, humor, and expressions that land in one country can sound absurd in another. A[study published in the Journal of International Marketing](https://www.ama.org/research-insights/research-insight-what-do-international-consumers-think-of-ai-translated-videos/) found that AI‑translated marketing videos were perceived as less natural than human translations, yet viewers were just as willing to like, share, or comment on them. A quick check by a native speaker helps when a video leans on dialogue.


Some formats barely need translation at all. Cooking, crafts, cleaning transformations, and DIY tutorials can cross borders on visuals alone.


## **Edits Can Help Creators Understand What's Working**


Meta also added an AI Assistant to **Edits** , its video app. The assistant reads Instagram performance data, including views, likes, shares, follower growth, and retention, then combines it with comments and audience interests to find patterns.


Instead of comparing spreadsheets, a creator can ask directly. Which Reels performed best recently. What the strongest ones have in common. Which topics generate shares. What to try next.


The answers are often small and useful. Short recipes may beat longer tutorials every time. One type of home organization video may pull far more non‑followers than anything else on the account. That is enough to decide which videos deserve a second audience.


The tool first rolled out to Edits users in the United States, so availability varies. Interpretation still belongs to the person making the videos.


## **What Happens When Your Reel Suddenly Becomes Popular Abroad?**


You open Insights and see something odd. A large share of viewers for your latest Reel are in a country you never targeted.


Maybe another creator shared it. Maybe the topic is popular there. Maybe the visuals work without words.


Before rewriting your whole strategy, look at what those viewers did. A jump in views is interesting. New followers, shares, profile visits, and people coming back say more about whether they want a second video.


Ways to build on it. Check Insights for where viewers come from and which videos draw them, and look for a pattern across several posts rather than one. Read the comments for repeated questions and inside jokes. Try AI translation if the language is supported, and review on‑screen text as well as captions. Make the profile readable for a stranger: a clear bio and a few pinned posts do most of the work. Then publish a related video and see whether the new audience returns. Trial Reels lets eligible creators test content with non‑followers before wider distribution.


Halbal and Dohmen crossed language barriers before any of these tools existed. The tools do not create that kind of moment. They make the audience it produces easier to notice, and easier to speak to.


For a small account, that is the interesting part. Somewhere, people may already like what you make.


You just have not reached them yet.
